summary: Specifies extensions to the Audio-Visual Profile with Feedback for codec control messages, helpful in conversational multimedia with central mixers. They cover things such as requesting a fresh video frame or limiting bit rate. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: In a video call, one side can send little notes like please send a fresh picture or please slow down. This defines those notes.

subtitle: Small RTCP messages that let video receivers and conference mixers ask senders for a fresh picture, a lower bit rate or a different quality trade-off.

tldr.problem: AVPF, the RTP profile for RTCP-based feedback, was built for point-to-point and small multipoint calls. Conferences that run through Multipoint Control Units (MCUs) need a few more feedback messages, and doing it through signaling such as SIP is too slow.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5104 adds six RTCP feedback messages: Full Intra Request, Temporal-Spatial Trade-off Request and Notification, a carrier for H.271 Video Back Channel Messages, and Temporary Maximum Media Stream Bit Rate Request and Notification. A new SDP value, ccm, negotiates which ones a session may use.
tldr.outcome: Senders, receivers and mixers get a fast media-path way to control video encoding. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7728 and RFC 8082.

today: RFC 5104 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7728 and RFC 8082; it has not been obsoleted. It builds on the AVPF profile in RFC 4585.

sections.title: Codec Control on Top of AVPF
sections.content:
When the Audio-Visual Profile with Feedback (AVPF, RFC 4585) was developed, the focus was on point-to-point and small multipoint calls without centralized control. In practice many small conferences run through Multipoint Control Units (MCUs), which in RTP terms are mixers and translators. Long experience in the conversational video industry suggested that a few additional feedback messages were needed to support them efficiently.

The RFC is explicit that it does not want to turn RTCP into a general control protocol. All of its messages are time-sensitive, have a simple fixed binary format and relate only to the RTP stream they are associated with. That is why it prefers them to slower signaling such as SIP. Understanding the memo also requires previous or parallel study of RFC 5117, which documents the RTP topologies it refers to.
sections.eli5: Video calls with many people go through a middle box. This RFC gives everyone a few quick, simple notes to send each other so the video stays good.

sections.title: Use Cases and Why the Media Path
sections.content:
The motivation section walks through use cases. A video mixer that adds a new source or switches to a different speaker needs a decoder refresh point from the new source. A user may want to slide between higher frame rate and higher picture quality. A mixer may need to lower the maximum bit rate an endpoint sends. A mobile receiver behind a cellular link may know its hard bit rate limit and want to tell the sender, so the sender does not probe beyond it. And a standardized feedback message from ITU-T Rec. H.271 needed a way to be carried.

The messages travel on the media path, in RTCP, for two stated reasons. MCUs often separate control from media processing, so media-path messages avoid extra traffic between the two parts. And signaling paths often pass through proxies and application servers that add delay.

Because RTCP is unreliable, each message type has its own rule for what happens when a message is lost, and for the case of multicast where receivers may send contradicting messages.
sections.eli5: A teacher in the middle of a group call can talk to each student faster by passing a note across the desk than by going through the principal's office.

sections.title: The Six New RTCP Messages
sections.content:
Two messages are transport layer feedback messages, with RTCP packet type RTPFB (205): TMMBR with FMT 3 and TMMBN with FMT 4. FMT 2 is marked reserved because early drafts of AVPF used it. Four are payload-specific feedback messages, with packet type PSFB (206): FIR with FMT 4, TSTR with FMT 5, TSTN with FMT 6 and VBCM with FMT 7.

In every one of them, the "SSRC of media source" field in the common header is not used and SHALL be set to 0. The SSRC of the media sender that a request applies to is carried inside each feedback control information (FCI) entry, so one message can address several media senders.

The RFC states design principles for the family: messages need strict real-time constraints, must be multicast-safe in that the reaction to contradicting messages is specified, and must relate to a codec or RTP stream. A two-way handshake is used only when an acknowledgement is required and cannot easily be derived from the media stream.
sections.eli5: There are six kinds of notes. Each has a number on the front so the receiver knows which kind it is, and each names the sender it is for.

sections.title: Asking for a Fresh Picture or a Different Trade-off
sections.content:
A Full Intra Request (FIR) is a command: the media sender MUST send a decoder refresh point as soon as possible. Each FCI entry has an SSRC, an 8-bit sequence number and 24 reserved bits. A repetition does not increase the sequence number, and a new command increases it by 1 modulo 256. FIR SHALL NOT be sent as a reaction to picture losses; the RFC recommends the AVPF Picture Loss Indication instead. Fitting uses are a new participant joining a conference or a switching MCU changing streams. The sender must still obey congestion control while sending the larger refresh picture, and a mixer acting on a FIR SHOULD issue its own rather than forward it.

The Temporal-Spatial Trade-off Request (TSTR) lets a receiver suggest an Index from 0 to 31. Zero asks for the highest spatial quality and 31 for the highest temporal resolution (frame rate). The index does not map to precise frame rates, and the request is a non-binding recommendation. The sender answers with a Temporal-Spatial Trade-off Notification (TSTN) that carries the index it will actually use. If several TSTRs have arrived from one requester, only the highest sequence number is answered.
sections.eli5: FIR is a bossy note: send a brand new full picture now. TSTR is a polite note: I would like smoother motion, or I would like sharper pictures, on a scale from 0 to 31, and the sender writes back what it will do.

sections.title: Capping the Bit Rate with TMMBR and TMMBN
sections.content:
The Temporary Maximum Media Stream Bit Rate Request (TMMBR, pronounced "timber") asks a sender to limit a media stream to a given maximum total media bit rate. Each request is a tuple of that maximum and the per-packet overhead the receiver has measured. The bit rate is sent as a 6-bit exponent and a 17-bit mantissa, where the rate in bits per second is mantissa * 2^exp. The overhead field is 9 bits, in bytes, and is a running average updated as 15/16 of the old value plus 1/16 of the latest packet's overhead.

The sender replies with a Temporary Maximum Media Stream Bit Rate Notification (TMMBN), which lists the bounding set: the most limiting tuples it has received, each tagged with the SSRC of its owner. Receivers use it to avoid sending requests that would not tighten the limit any further. A TMMBN SHALL be sent after any TMMBR that names the sender, even if the new tuple was not accepted into the bounding set.

A TMMBR can never push a sender above the bit rate negotiated in signaling. Any increase has to be governed by congestion control, and it is made only after a delay following the TMMBN that announces the higher limit, so that other participants can report lower limits. If a new limit is likely to hold for the rest of the session, the RFC expects a renegotiation through session signaling.
sections.eli5: Everyone on a group call tells the sender the most data they can handle. The sender keeps the smallest number and tells everybody which limit is the strictest, so nobody has to repeat a looser request.

sections.title: Carrying H.271 Video Back Channel Messages
sections.content:
The Video Back Channel Message (VBCM) transparently carries a feedback message defined by ITU-T Rec. H.271 from receiver to sender. Each FCI entry holds the target SSRC, a sequence number, a 7-bit RTP payload type that says how to interpret the bit string, a 16-bit length, the octet string itself and padding to a 32-bit boundary.

Because some H.271 messages are not safe when many receivers can send them, the RFC sets rules. Implementations MUST respect congestion control and SHOULD prefer the native IETF messages where the H.271 message is equivalent, such as a picture loss message or a refresh point. They MUST NOT use H.271 messages with multicast, and MUST NOT use them in centralized multipoint scenarios, unless the implementer fully understands the issues the RFC lists, such as different decoder state on different receivers.
sections.eli5: This is an envelope that lets a video codec's own note travel inside the call. The RFC mostly says to use its own simpler notes when they mean the same thing.

sections.title: Negotiating Support in SDP
sections.content:
Support is negotiated through the rtcp-fb attribute from AVPF. RFC 5104 adds a new feedback value, ccm, followed by a parameter naming the supported message: fir, tmmbr, tstr or vbcm. The tmmbr parameter has an optional smaxpr= sub-parameter for the session maximum packet rate, which defaults to infinity. vbcm takes zero or more H.271 sub-message types.

In an offer/answer exchange, the answerer MUST remove any ccm parameters it does not support and MUST NOT add new ones. Only the joint subset may be used. For example, an offer can list a=rtcp-fb:98 ccm fir and a=rtcp-fb:98 ccm tstr for an H.263 video stream.

IANA registered the value ccm and created a registry of ccm parameters, with new entries following the "Specification required" policy.
sections.eli5: Before the call, each side lists which kinds of notes it understands. The call may only use the kinds that both sides listed.

sections.title: Congestion and Security
sections.content:
Correct AVPF timing rules keep feedback messages from flooding the network, but the messages change sender behavior, and that behavior MUST respect congestion control. For example, the many packets of a refresh picture sent after a FIR have to be paced by the congestion control algorithm, even if the user sees slow recovery.

Spoofed or malicious feedback can do real damage: a false TMMBR can cut the bit rate severely, a forged TMMBN can assign a bounding tuple to the wrong participant, bad TSTRs can degrade the picture, and repeated FIRs can make the video jerky. The RFC requires authentication and integrity protection of the setup signaling and calls for the same protection for the feedback messages, for example with the SAVPF profile that combines Secure RTP and AVPF. In mixer setups, separate security contexts can protect other users from a misbehaving participant.
sections.eli5: If a stranger can slip fake notes into the call, they could make your video blurry or choppy, so the notes have to be locked so only people on the call can send them.

fields.desc: Command sequence number, increased by 1 modulo 256 for each new command; repetitions keep it.

fields.desc: Set to 0 by the sender and ignored on reception.

fields.name: SSRC
fields.desc: The media sender asked to apply the trade-off.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 by the sender and ignored on reception.

fields.name: Index
fields.desc: 0 asks for the highest spatial quality, 31 for the highest temporal resolution.

fields.name: SSRC
fields.desc: The media sender asked to obey the new maximum bit rate.

fields.name: MxTBR Exp
fields.desc: Exponent for the maximum total media bit rate, 0 to 63.

fields.name: MxTBR Mantissa
fields.desc: Mantissa of the maximum total media bit rate.

fields.name: Measured Overhead
fields.desc: Measured average packet overhead in bytes, 0 to 511.
